extracted.intended_audience: students of differential equations / dynamical systems (advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, definitions, and canonical-form procedures for classifying linear systems (planar and higher-dimensional) by eigenvalues, trace/determinant, conjugacy, hyperbolicity, and canonical blocks. Includes algebraic prerequisites (determinant, invertibility, eigenvectors) and real canonical form for complex eigenpairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace–determinant plane as bifurcation diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: The trace–determinant (T–D) plane is the analogue of the bifurcation diagram for planar linear systems: a one-parameter family corresponds to a curve in the TD-plane, and when this curve crosses the T-axis, the positive D-axis, or the parabola T^2 − 4D = 0, the phase portrait undergoes a bifurcation (a major change in geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the TD-plane to visualize parameter changes: track where the family-curve crosses those loci to detect qualitative changes in phase portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick classification from D and T
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain qualitative features can be deduced from trace T and determinant D without computing eigenvalues: e.g., D < 0 implies a saddle at the origin; if both D and T are positive then the origin is a source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply sign tests on D and T to rapidly identify saddle/source/sink regions in the TD-plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological conjugacy (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two systems X' = AX and X' = BX are (topologically) conjugate if there exists a homeomorphism h: R^2 → R^2 such that φ_B(t, h(X0)) = h(φ_A(t, X0)) for all t and initial X0 (i.e., h carries solution curves/flows of one system onto those of the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: h must be one-to-one, onto, continuous with continuous inverse; conjugacy preserves qualitative (topological) fate of solutions, not necessarily metric or differentiable structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-dimensional conjugacy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For 1D linear systems x' = λ1 x and x' = λ2 x (both nonzero), they are conjugate iff λ1 and λ2 have the same sign. An explicit homeomorphism is given (piecewise) by h(x) = x^{λ2/λ1} with the sign convention for x<0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same sign of eigenvalues ensures same asymptotic fate (both tend to or away from origin); differing signs prevent a global homeomorphism (would map 0 to infinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow homeomorphism (not diffeomorphism) for conjugacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugacies are required to be homeomorphisms only (continuous with continuous inverse), not diffeomorphisms. If differentiability were required, then in simple 1D cases λ1 = λ2 would be forced, which is too restrictive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-differentiability at points (e.g., origin) is acceptable for topological conjugacy; this broadens equivalence classes to capture qualitative similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic matrix / system (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A matrix A is hyperbolic if none of its eigenvalues has real part 0; the system X' = AX is called hyperbolic in this case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbolicity excludes center-type (purely imaginary / zero real part) behaviors and enables robust classification by sign of real parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy criterion for hyperbolic 2×2 systems (main theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two hyperbolic 2×2 linear systems X' = A_i X are conjugate if and only if each matrix has the same number of eigenvalues with negative real part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields three conjugacy classes for planar hyperbolic systems: (1) one eigenvalue positive and one negative (saddle), (2) both eigenvalues with negative real parts (sink), (3) both eigenvalues with positive real parts (source). Systems within the same class are topologically equivalent though their phase portraits may appear different (e.g., spiral vs real sink).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of conjugacy in saddle case
rubrics_metrics.description: If each matrix has eigenvalues λ_i < 0 < μ_i (saddle), use separate 1D conjugacies for the λ and μ directions (h1 and h2) and define H(x,y) = (h1(x), h2(y)) to produce a conjugacy between the 2D systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to product of one-dimensional problems along invariant eigendirections; conjugacy acts coordinatewise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy to −I for sinks/sources (non-Jordan case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a planar canonical-form matrix A has both eigenvalues with negative real parts and is not the defective Jordan form [λ 1; 0 λ], then A is conjugate to B = −I. Proof constructs a conjugacy via the unit circle S^1, the 'time-to-hit' function τ(x,y) when solutions meet S^1, and mapping forward/back along flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the vector field points inward on S^1 (AX(θ)·N(θ)<0), define τ by implicit function theorem (continuity/differentiability), then assemble homeomorphism H(x,y)=φ_B^{−τ}∘φ_A^{τ}(x,y). This establishes topological equivalence to radial exponential contraction (−I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Jordan-block (defective) case via change of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = [λ 1; 0 λ] (with λ < 0), a suitable linear change of variables T (a shear with small parameter ε > 0 chosen so ε < −λ) transforms A into a form whose vector field points inside S^1, reducing to the previous case and yielding conjugacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an explicit invertible T to remove the obstruction to inward-pointing field; choose parameters small enough to guarantee AX·N < 0 on S^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant/invertibility criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An n×n matrix A is invertible iff det A ≠ 0. Equivalently, A is invertible iff the linear system AX = V has a unique solution for every V ∈ R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Row-reduce A to triangular form: invertibility ↔ no zero diagonal entries; determinants of elementary row operations explain how det changes during reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of elementary row operations on determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Row operation effects on determinant: (1) adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged; (2) swapping two rows multiplies det by −1; (3) multiplying a row by k multiplies det by k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these facts when computing determinants via row operations or understanding how elementary matrices affect det (det(LA) = det L · det A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant of triangular matrix
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is upper or lower triangular, then det A equals the product of the diagonal entries (a11 ··· ann).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful shortcut when matrix already triangular (or after row-reduction) to compute det quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicativity of determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: For n×n matrices A and B, det(AB) = (det A)(det B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either A or B is noninvertible the identity holds trivially (both sides zero); otherwise prove via factorization into elementary matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Columns linearly independent ↔ invertible
rubrics_metrics.description: A is invertible if and only if its column vectors form a linearly independent set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If columns are dependent then AZ = 0 has nontrivial solution so A noninvertible; conversely invertibility implies uniqueness of solutions and thus column independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalue definition via characteristic polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: λ is an eigenvalue of A iff det(A − λI) = 0; since det(A − λI) is an n-th degree polynomial, there are exactly n roots counted with algebraic multiplicity (over C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characteristic polynomial to locate eigenvalues (real or complex) and to infer multiplicities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct real eigenvalues ⇒ independent eigenvectors (diagonalizability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If λ1,...,λn are real and distinct eigenvalues of A with associated eigenvectors V1,...,Vn, then the Vj are linearly independent; thus A is diagonalizable over R with T formed by eigenvectors so that T^{-1}AT = diag(λ1,...,λn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct T with columns equal to eigenvectors; invertibility of T follows from independence; useful for explicit solution of linear ODEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex eigenpairs produce real 2×2 blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: If α + iβ is a (nonreal) eigenvalue with eigenvector V, then its complex conjugate α − iβ and conjugate eigenvector appear as well. The real and imaginary parts of V (W_{2j−1} = Re V, W_{2j} = Im V) are real and linearly independent; in that real basis the corresponding block is Dj = [[α, β], [−β, α]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real and imaginary parts of complex eigenvectors to form an invertible T with real columns; T^{-1}AT becomes block-diagonal with 2×2 rotation–scaling blocks representing complex eigenpairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical block form for matrix with distinct eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: If A has distinct eigenvalues (real and/or complex), one can choose an invertible T so that T^{-1}AT is block-diagonal with 1×1 blocks λ_i for real eigenvalues and 2×2 blocks Dj = [[α_j, β_j], [−β_j, α_j]] for each complex conjugate pair α_j ± iβ_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This real canonical form generalizes diagonalization and gives the normal forms used to classify linear flows in higher dimensions (distinct eigenvalues assumed).
